title: 10. Security & Auth: OAuth 2.0
summary: OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) is a delegated authorization framework that lets a resource owner grant a client application limited access to their resources on a resource server, without sharing their credentials, by routing the user…
objectives: What problem does OAuth 2.0 solve that password-sharing did not?
What are the four OAuth roles, and how do they map to a real "Log in with Google" flow?
What is PKCE, and why is it now required for SPAs and mobile apps?
What is the difference between the authorization code, implicit, password, and client credentials flows, and which should you use?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) is a delegated authorization framework that lets a resource owner grant a client application limited access to their resources on a resource server, without sharing their credentials, by routing the user through an authorization server that issues scoped, short-lived access tokens.

OAuth 2.0 was published in 2012 to solve a problem that had become universal on the early web: third-party applications wanted to access a user's data on another service — print photos from Flickr, post tweets from a scheduling tool, read a user's Google Calendar — but the only way to do it was for the user to hand their password to the third-party app. This was catastrophic for security (the app could do anything the user could do, including changing the password) and for privacy (the app saw everything, not just the requested scope). OAuth 2.0 replaced password sharing with a delegation model: the user authenticates only with their identity provider, the provider issues a scoped token to the third-party app, and the app uses the token to access only the resources the user authorized. By 2024, "Log in with Google," "Sign in with Apple," and "Continue with Facebook" buttons — all powered by OAuth 2.0 — were the dominant identity pattern for consumer apps, with billions of daily authentications.

The framework defines four roles. The **resource owner** is the user who owns the data. The **client** is the third-party application that wants to access the data. The **authorization server** is the OAuth provider that authenticates the user and issues tokens. The **resource server** is the API that hosts the user's data and accepts tokens. The flow is conceptually simple: the client redirects the user to the authorization server, the user logs in and approves the requested scopes, the authorization server redirects back to the client with an authorization code, and the client exchanges the code (plus its client secret) for an access token at a back-channel endpoint. The access token is then sent as a `Bearer` token on every API call to the resource server. This indirection means the user's password never reaches the client, the client receives only the scopes it was granted, and the authorization server can revoke the token at any time. The trade-off is complexity: OAuth 2.0 has multiple flows, edge cases around token storage and refresh, and a long history of implementation footguns.

The **authorization code flow** (with PKCE, pronounced "pixie") is the only flow recommended for new applications in 2024. The client redirects the user to the authorization server's `/authorize` endpoint with a `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `scope`, `state` (CSRF token), and a `code_challenge` (PKCE). After the user logs in and consents, the server redirects back to the client's `redirect_uri` with an authorization code. The client POSTs the code plus its `code_verifier` (PKCE) to `/token`, and receives an access token (and usually a refresh token). PKCE (RFC 7636) was added because the original flow assumed the client could keep a static `client_secret` — true for server-side apps but impossible for SPAs and mobile apps, where the secret is extractable. PKCE replaces the static secret with a per-request challenge/verifier pair, so even if the authorization code is intercepted (e.g., via a malicious redirect_uri or a custom-scheme interception on mobile), the attacker cannot redeem it without the verifier. Google, Microsoft, GitHub, and Auth0 all require PKCE for SPA and mobile clients as of 2023.

The **client credentials flow** is for service-to-service authorization: a backend service authenticates with its own `client_id` and `client_secret` (or mTLS) and receives an access token scoped to its own identity, with no user involved. This is how microservices talk to each other, how a CI/CD pipeline deploys to a cloud API, and how AWS Cognito machine-to-machine authentication works. The **device authorization grant** (RFC 8628, used by `gcloud`, `gh`, and `aws sso login`) is for devices without a keyboard: the device displays a user code and a URL, the user opens a browser on another device to enter the code, and the original device polls the token endpoint until the user completes authentication. The **resource owner password credentials** flow (ROPC), where the client collects the user's password and exchanges it directly for a token, was deprecated by OAuth 2.1 because it defeats delegation. The **implicit flow**, which returned the access token directly in the redirect URL fragment, was also deprecated because tokens in URLs leak via browser history and referrer headers; SPAs should use authorization code with PKCE instead.

Scopes are the mechanism by which the user grants fine-grained consent. A scope is a string identifier (e.g., `calendar.read`, `profile`, `email`, `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.send`) that the client requests and the user approves or denies. The issued access token is bound to the granted scopes, and the resource server enforces them on every request. The principle of minimal scope applies: a client should request only the scopes it needs. Real-world examples: Google's `Sign in with Google` button requests `openid email profile` (three scopes for federated login); the Gmail API scopes distinguish read-only (`gmail.readonly`) from send-only (`gmail.send`) so a mail-merge app cannot read incoming mail. Consent screens — the "App X wants to access your Y" prompts — surface scopes as human-readable descriptions, which is why Google and Microsoft invest heavily in scope naming and per-app review.

Tokens come in two flavors. **Access tokens** are short-lived (5–60 minutes for Google, 1 hour for AWS Cognito) and are presented to the resource server on every API call. They are typically JWTs (see Topic 3) signed by the authorization server, though opaque tokens validated via introspection (RFC 7662) are also valid. **Refresh tokens** are long-lived (days to weeks) and silently obtain new access tokens without re-prompting the user. Refresh tokens are server-side and revocable, which is the only way to "log out" a user from an OAuth session short of waiting for the access token to expire. Refresh-token rotation, where each refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, adds theft detection: replay of a stolen old refresh token triggers revocation of the entire session family. The trade-off is operational complexity — clients must handle silent refresh, multi-tab refresh races, and revoked refresh tokens.

The most common OAuth 2.0 vulnerabilities are redirect-URI manipulation, scope confusion, and token leakage. Redirect-URI attacks exploit permissive matching rules: if the server accepts any redirect URI whose prefix matches the registered one, an attacker can register `https://attacker.com.evil.com/` and intercept the authorization code. The mitigation is exact-match redirect URIs and the `state` parameter as a CSRF token. Scope confusion happens when the resource server does not validate the scopes in the token, so a token minted with `read` scope is accepted for `write`. Token leakage happens when access tokens end up in URLs (browser history, referrer headers, proxy logs), in localStorage (XSS-exfiltratable), or in mobile deep-link handlers. OAuth 2.0 Security BCP (RFC 9700) codifies the mitigations: exact-match redirect URIs, PKCE, `state`, HttpOnly cookies or platform keystores for token storage, never log tokens, back-channel token exchange. Production providers — Google, Microsoft, Auth0, Okta — implement these by default, but every client integration is a place to introduce a bug.

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant U as User (Resource Owner) participant C as Client App participant AS as Authorization Server participant RS as Resource Server U->>C: Click "Connect my Google Calendar" C->>C: Generate PKCE verifier + challenge C->>U: Redirect to AS /authorize?
client_id, redirect_uri, scope,
state, code_challenge U->>AS: Browser follows redirect AS->>U: Show login + consent screen U->>AS: Login + approve scopes AS->>U: Redirect to client redirect_uri
?code=AUTH_CODE&state=... U->>C: Browser arrives at client with code C->>AS: POST /token (code, code_verifier, client_id) AS->>AS: Verify code, PKCE verifier, client AS-->>C: access_token (JWT, 1h) + refresh_token (7d) C->>RS: GET /calendars (Authorization: Bearer ) RS->>RS: Verify token + scopes RS-->>C: 200 OK + calendar data Note over C,AS: 1h later: silent refresh using refresh_token ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +------+ click +---------+ | User | -------------> | Client | +------+ | App | ^ +----+----+ | | | 1. redirect to AS | 2. /authorize? | /authorize | client_id+scope v v +-------------------+ +-------------------+ | Authorization | | User authenticates| | Server (Google) |<--| + approves scopes | +---------+---------+ +-------------------+ | | 3. redirect to client's redirect_uri | ?code=AUTH_CODE&state=CSRF v +---------+---------+ | Client App | | 4. POST /token | | code+verifier | +---------+---------+ | | 5. access_token + refresh_token v +---------+---------+ 6. GET /api with Bearer +-----------+ | Client (server | -------------------------> | Resource | | side, secret- | <------------------------- | Server | | safe) | 200 OK | (Google | +-------------------+ | Calendar)| +-----------+ ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The user clicks "Connect my Calendar" in the client app; the client generates a PKCE verifier and challenge, persists the verifier, and redirects the user's browser to the authorization server's `/authorize` endpoint with `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `scope`, `state`, and `code_challenge`. 2. The authorization server prompts the user to log in and to approve the requested scopes (consent screen); the user's credentials never reach the client. 3. The authorization server redirects the browser back to the client's `redirect_uri` with an authorization code and the original `state` value, which the client verifies to defeat CSRF. 4. The client POSTs the code plus the PKCE `code_verifier` (and its `client_secret` if it is a confidential client) to the `/token` endpoint over the back channel. 5. The authorization server verifies the code, the PKCE verifier (hashes to the original challenge), and the client identity, then returns a short-lived access JWT plus a long-lived refresh token. 6. The client uses the access JWT as a `Bearer` token on every call to the resource server; when it expires, the client silently exchanges the refresh token for a new access JWT.

quiz.explanation: Before OAuth, third-party apps that wanted to access a user's data on another service had to ask the user for their password on that service. This was catastrophic: the app could do anything the user could do (including changing the password), the app saw everything rather than the specific data it needed, and the user had no way to revoke access short of changing their password.

quiz.explanation: PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, RFC 7636) replaces the static client_secret with a per-request challenge/verifier pair. The client generates a random code_verifier (43–128 characters), computes code_challenge = base64url(sha256(verifier)), and sends the challenge in the /authorize request. The authorization server stores the challenge alongside the issued code.
